blocks.content: 1. MEANING OF ECONOMIC PLANNING

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Economic planning in India commenced with the creation of the Planning Commission in 1950 under Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru.
The First Five-Year Plan (1951–1956) was based on the Harrod-Domar Model with a primary focus on agriculture.
The Second Five-Year Plan (1956–1961) adopted the PC Mahalanobis Model, prioritizing heavy industries and public sector expansion.
NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission on 1st January 2015, shifting India's policy model towards cooperative federalism.
The 12th Five-Year Plan (2012–2017) was India's last Five-Year Plan, aimed at faster, sustainable, and inclusive growth.

blocks.content: Economic Planning refers to a systematic and organized effort by the government to allocate resources efficiently in order to achieve specific economic goals such as growth, employment, poverty reduction and industrial development.
India adopted planned economic development after independence to overcome poverty, low industrial base, unemployment and regional imbalance.
2. OBJECTIVES OF ECONOMIC PLANNING IN INDIA
3. PLANNING COMMISSION (1950–2014)
Planning Commission was established in 1950 by a Government of India resolution.

Chairperson: Prime Minister

Function: Formulate Five-Year Plans and allocate resources.
It was replaced by NITI Aayog in 2015.
4. NITI AAYOG (FROM 2015)
NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India) was formed on 1 January 2015.
It promotes cooperative federalism and acts as a policy think tank.
5. FIVE-YEAR PLANS IN INDIA
6. TYPES OF PLANNING

• Centralized Planning – Decisions taken by central authority.

• Indicative Planning – Market plays major role, government gives direction.

• Perspective Planning – Long-term goals (15–20 years).
7. ACHIEVEMENTS & LIMITATIONS

Achievements:

• Growth in agriculture and industry

• Expansion of infrastructure

• Reduction in poverty levels



Limitations:

• Slow growth in early years

• License Raj issues

• Regional imbalance
8.FIVE-YEAR PLANS
1st Five-Year Plan (1951–1956)

Focus: Agriculture, Irrigation, Community Development

Model: Harrod-Domar Model

Objective: Food security & rehabilitation after partition

Growth Target: 2.1% | Achieved: ~3.6%

Major Achievement: Bhakra-Nangal Dam, focus on rural development
2nd Five-Year Plan (1956–1961)

Focus: Heavy Industries

Model: Mahalanobis Model

Objective: Rapid industrialisation

Growth Target: 4.5% | Achieved: ~4.3%

Major Achievement: Establishment of steel plants (Bhilai, Durgapur, Rourkela)
3rd Five-Year Plan (1961–1966)

Focus: Self-reliance & agriculture

Objective: Increase food production

Growth Target: 5.6% | Achieved: ~2.4%

Issues: Indo-China war, Indo-Pak war, drought
Plan Holiday (1966–1969)

rows: Had power to allocate funds to states and ministries
Advisory Think Tank without fund allocation powers
Limited to National Development Council interactions
Active participation via the Governing Council

blocks.content:
Three Annual Plans due to economic crisis

Focus: Agriculture & price stability

Green Revolution initiated
4th Five-Year Plan (1969–1974)

Focus: Growth with stability & self-reliance

Objective: Reduce inflation

Major Step: Nationalisation of banks (1969)
5th Five-Year Plan (1974–1979)

Focus: Poverty removal (Garibi Hatao)

Objective: Self-reliance & employment

Terminated early in 1978
6th Five-Year Plan (1980–1985)

Focus: Poverty alleviation & technology

Objective: Reduce unemployment

Major Program: IRDP (Integrated Rural Development Programme)
7th Five-Year Plan (1985–1990)

Focus: Food, work & productivity

Objective: Strengthen agriculture & employment

Emphasis on modernization
8th Five-Year Plan (1992–1997)

Focus: Human development & liberalisation

Context: Post-1991 economic reforms

Growth Achieved: ~6.8%

Major Shift: Market-oriented reforms
9th Five-Year Plan (1997–2002)

Focus: Growth with social justice

Objective: Employment generation

Emphasis on agriculture & rural development

items: The 1st Five-Year Plan used the Harrod-Domar Model, while the 2nd Five-Year Plan followed the Mahalanobis Model.
Plan Holidays occurred between 1966 and 1969 due to the Sino-Indian War, Indo-Pak War, and severe droughts.
The Prime Minister of India acts as the ex-officio Chairperson of NITI Aayog.
NITI Aayog follows a 'Bottom-Up' planning model, unlike the 'Top-Down' model of the Planning Commission.

blocks.content: 10th Five-Year Plan (2002–2007)

Focus: Faster & more inclusive growth

Target Growth: 8% per annum

Emphasis: Infrastructure & poverty reduction
11th Five-Year Plan (2007–2012)

Focus: Inclusive growth

Objective: Education, health & skill development

Target Growth: 9% | Achieved: ~8%
12th Five-Year Plan (2012–2017)

Focus: Faster, sustainable & inclusive growth

Target Growth: 8%

Emphasis: Infrastructure, energy & environment

Last Five-Year Plan; Planning Commission replaced by NITI Aayog in 2015
RRB HIGH-VALUE SUMMARY POINTS

• 1st Plan – Agriculture focus

• 2nd Plan – Mahalanobis Model (Heavy Industry)

• Green Revolution during Plan Holiday

• 8th Plan – Post-LPG reforms

• 12th Plan – Last Five-Year Plan

• Planning Commission established in 1950.

• NITI Aayog formed in 2015.

• 2nd Plan based on Mahalanobis Model.

• 8th Plan linked with economic reforms.
